title: CS 209: For Loops
description: for loops: counting passes, accumulating, scope and braces, ++ / += / -=, mixed with concatenation and integer division. Lecture 10-6.

cards.definition: Repeats a step many times instead of writing it out again and again.
for: you know how many times to repeat. while / do-while: you don't know in advance.
for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) { ... } — start the counter, keep going while the test is true, change the counter each time.

cards.term: Order a for loop runs in
cards.definition: init (once) → test → body → update → test → body → update … until the test is false.
int i = 0; — runs exactly once, before the first test.
i < 5 — checked before EVERY pass, including the first. False → the loop ends.
Same as i = i - 1. Used to count down.
Same as i = i + 2. Also works with a variable: total += price.
Comparison operators. <= and >= put the = second; =< and => don't compile.
A variable that builds up a result across passes: int sum = 0; then sum += i; inside the loop.
Put the println AFTER the loop's closing brace to print the final total once.
for (int i = a; i < b; i++) runs b - a times; with <= it runs b - a + 1 times.
Without { }, only the FIRST statement after the for repeats.
A counter declared in the for (int i = ...) only exists inside the loop. Using i after it won't compile.

questions.prompt: How many times does the body run?
questions.explanation: i takes 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. At 5 the test i < 5 is false, so it stops: 5 passes.

questions.prompt: How many times does the body run?
questions.explanation: i takes 0 through 5 because <= includes 5: that's 6 values.

questions.prompt: How many times does the body run?
questions.explanation: i is 1, 4, 7, 10. The next value, 13, fails i <= 10.

questions.prompt: How many times does the body run?
questions.explanation: The test is checked BEFORE the first pass: 5 < 5 is false, so the body never runs.

questions.prompt: In what order do the parts of a for loop run?
choices: init once, then test → body → update, repeating
questions.answer: init once, then test → body → update, repeating
questions.explanation: The init runs exactly once. The test comes before every pass, which is why a loop can run zero times.

questions.prompt: You keep asking for passwords until one is right. Which kind of loop fits best?
choices: A while loop: you don't know how many tries it'll take
A for loop: it always fits
A for loop, because it has a counter
No loop; write the check 10 times
questions.answer: A while loop: you don't know how many tries it'll take
questions.explanation: for is for a known number of repeats. When you can't know the count in advance, that's the while / do-while kind (syntax coming later).

choices: Adds total to price and stores it in price
questions.explanation: x += y is shorthand for x = x + y. The variable on the left is the one that changes.

questions.prompt: Which test means "keep going while i is at most 10"?
questions.explanation: The = goes second: <=. i < 10 stops one early (at 9), and =< isn't an operator at all.
The ; right after the for( ) is an empty loop body: the loop runs 3 times doing nothing. The { } block is a separate statement that runs once afterwards.
No braces: only the first statement (print a) repeats. print b runs once, after the loop.

questions.prompt: You want to print the final sum ONCE. Where does the println go?
choices: Inside the loop, after sum += i
questions.explanation: Inside the loop it would print every partial sum. After the closing brace, the loop has finished and sum holds the total.

choices: It won't compile: i only exists inside the loop
questions.answer: It won't compile: i only exists inside the loop
questions.explanation: i is declared in the for( ), so its scope is the loop. Line 4 uses a name that no longer exists.
i + i is number + number, so it adds (2, 4, 6) before the " " turns it into text.
sum is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. 10 / 4 is int / int = 2 before it's stored, so 2.0.
Semicolons separate the three parts, => isn't an operator, and Java is case-sensitive (for, not For).
print(i) leaves the cursor on the line, then println("*") adds * and ends the line. No space is printed between them.

questions.code:
for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++)
    System.out.print(i);
questions.explanation: Starts at 0 and stops before 4. With no spaces printed, the digits run together.
Counts down from 5; at 0 the test i > 0 is false. (Trailing spaces don't matter when you type it.)
i is 0, 3, 6, 9; the next value, 12, fails i < 10.
println ends each line, so each row is on its own line.
"" first makes it text, so i is appended twice: 11, 22, 33.
10, 7, 4, 1. The next value would be -2, which fails i > 0.
3 + 4 + 5 + 6 = 18, printed once after the loop.
The println is INSIDE the loop, so it prints the running total each pass: 1, 1+2, 1+2+3.
% 3 cycles 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, 0 as i goes up.
c + i is char + int = a number (97 + i), and that's done before the " " joins.

questions.prompt: After this runs, what is the value of s?
questions.explanation: Each new digit goes on the FRONT: "1", then "21", then "321".

questions.prompt: After this runs, what is the value of a?
questions.explanation: 0 + 1 + 4 + 9 = 14 (* happens before +=).

questions.prompt: After this runs, what is the value of avg?
questions.explanation: sum is 10, and 10 / 4 is integer division (2) before it's stored: 2.0. Use 4.0 to get 2.5.

questions.prompt: After this runs, what is the value of y?
questions.explanation: Without braces only x++ is in the loop. y++ runs once afterwards, however it's indented.
i was declared in the for( ), so it doesn't exist after the loop's closing brace.
The three parts of a for header are separated by semicolons, not commas.
=> isn't an operator in Java. "Greater than or equal" is >=.
sum += i means sum = sum + i, and sum never got a starting value. Start accumulators at 0.
i is never declared. The init needs a type: int i = 0.
i already exists inside the loop (declared in the header), so it can't be declared again.

questions.prompt: This compiles. Which line crashes when it runs?
questions.explanation: On the very first pass i is 0, so total / i divides by zero. It compiles fine and crashes at runtime.
The for header's ( ) is never closed.
